AI-optimized server spending is on track to triple traditional server spending by 2027. The cloud-everything era is getting a serious counterweight.

That calculus has changed. Organizations that graduated from pilot projects to production workloads are now processing tens of millions of tokens daily. At that scale, per-token cloud pricing starts looking less like convenience and more like a recurring tax with no end date. Egress costs alone add 15 to 30 percent on top of the already steep token fees.

The numbers back up the market demand. HPE signed $1.1 billion in net new AI systems orders in a single quarter, exiting with a $3.2 billion backlog. One-third of those orders came from enterprises, not hyperscalers. Air-gapped deployment is now available with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs.
Lenovo’s 2026 TCO study compared a production inference workload processing 10 billion tokens per month over three years:

The decision threshold is fairly clean. Below 10 million tokens per day, cloud reserved instances typically win on total cost when you include the 0.5 FTE staff needed to manage on-premises hardware ($225,000 to $300,000 over three years). Above 50 million tokens per day, on-premises is almost always financially superior.

GPU prices have dropped enough to accelerate this math. H100 SXMs settled at $25,000 to $30,000 (down from $35,000 to $40,000 in 2023). A100s now run $8,000 to $12,000. A full 3-year TCO for an 8x H100 server, including staffing, lands between $712,000 and $948,000. Compare that to the equivalent cloud spend at production volume, and the gap is hard to ignore.

Worth noting: AI and ML workloads already represent 22% of total cloud costs at SaaS and IT companies according to the FinOps Foundation. That is a massive line item, and it only goes in one direction.

“ibm losing $40b because claude can read cobol is a massive overreaction. current models have always understood cobol; the real bottleneck isn’t the ‘translation,’ it’s the secure, on-prem execution. no major bank is sending their core financial logic to a public api.”

Someone has to keep these machines running. The Lenovo TCO model allocates 0.5 FTE at $75,000 to $100,000 per year. That is optimistic for a team managing GPU clusters, model deployments, and security patches across air-gapped infrastructure.

Liquid-cooled GPU servers draw serious wattage. A rack of 8x H100s consumes roughly 10 kW. At $0.10 per kWh, that is $8,760 per year per rack just in electricity, before cooling costs. Dell’s new XE9812 with NVL72 is fully liquid-cooled and fanless, which helps, but the facility still needs plumbing upgrades.

The cost math only works at high utilization rates. A $950,000 server cluster running at 10% utilization is an expensive paperweight. Cloud APIs have zero utilization risk because you only pay for what you use.

The trajectory is clear. IDC reported 166% year-over-year growth in compute and storage hardware spending for AI in Q2 2025. Gartner expects datacenter systems spending to hit $489.5 billion in 2025, up 46.8% from 2024. The vendors are shipping hardware specifically designed for this moment.
